summary: Describes how to produce digital signatures and hashes using the GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94 algorithms for DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS records in DNSSEC. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC signs addresses so they can't be faked. This describes using a particular country's signing recipes. It is now historic.

subtitle: How to sign DNS data and make DS digests with the Russian GOST algorithms in DNSSEC.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC's algorithm list in RFC 4034 did not include the Russian GOST signature and hash algorithms, so zones could not be signed with them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds GOST R 34.10-2001 signatures as DNSSEC algorithm number 12 and the GOST R 34.11-94 hash as DS digest type 3, and says how to store keys and build signatures and digests.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is now Historic and was updated by RFC 6944, so it is not a current recommendation for new DNSSEC deployments.

today: RFC 5933 is Historic and was updated by RFC 6944. It is no longer a current specification for DNSSEC algorithm choice, though the text still records how algorithm 12 and digest type 3 were defined.

sections.title: Why GOST Needed a DNSSEC Specification
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds cryptographic keys and digital signatures to the Domain Name System so that clients can check the authenticity and integrity of DNS data. RFC 4034 says how to store DNSKEY and RRSIG records and lists the algorithms that may be used.

This document extends that list with the signature algorithm GOST R 34.10-2001 and the hash algorithm GOST R 34.11-94. It explains how to store the key data and how to produce RRSIG records with them. The RFC assumes the reader already knows DNSSEC and the GOST algorithms.

The term "GOST" is not officially defined. It usually names a group of Russian cryptographic algorithms, but in this document it means only GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94, because GOST 28147-89 is not used in DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS has a list of approved ways to sign its answers. This RFC adds one more way to the list and explains exactly how to use it.

sections.title: GOST Keys in DNSKEY Records
sections.content:
GOST R 34.10-2001 public keys are stored in DNSKEY records with algorithm number 12. The wire format is compatible with RFC 4491. A public key is a point on an elliptic curve, written Q = (x,y).

On the wire the key MUST be 64 octets: the first 32 octets hold x and the second 32 octets hold y, both in little-endian form. The key parameters are the ones named id-GostR3410-2001-CryptoPro-A-ParamSet, and the digest parameters are id-GostR3411-94-CryptoProParamSet.

Existing GOST-aware libraries could read keys through a generic X509 interface if the key is encoded as in RFC 4491. To get that encoding, the RFC says to put a fixed 37-byte sequence in front of the 64 key octets. It also gives a worked example of a private key and the DNSKEY record for example.net that goes with it.
sections.plainLanguage: A GOST key is a pair of two big numbers, glued together into one 64-byte block. The RFC says which number goes first and how to write the bytes.

sections.title: Signatures in RRSIG Records
sections.content:
To sign a set of records, the signer first hashes the wire-format data of the record set with GOST R 34.11-94, written hash = GOSTR3411(data). The hash MUST use the parameters named id-GostR3411-94-CryptoProParamSet.

The signature is then computed from that hash with GOST R 34.10-2001. Its wire format follows RFC 4490: two 256-bit numbers, r and s, written as 64 octets, with s in the first 32 octets and r in the second 32, both big-endian. The other RRSIG fields are as in RFC 4034.

The RFC includes an example that signs an A record for www.example.net. It notes that the algorithm uses random data, so a real signature will differ each time it is calculated.
sections.plainLanguage: First the data is squashed into a short fingerprint. Then the fingerprint is stamped with the secret key, and anyone with the public key can check the stamp.

sections.title: GOST Digests in DS Records
sections.content:
A DS record in a parent zone points at a child zone's key. This RFC denotes the GOST R 34.11-94 digest algorithm in DS records by digest type 3. The digest value is in little-endian form, compatible with RFC 4490, and MUST always be computed with the id-GostR3411-94-CryptoProParamSet parameters.

The example takes a key-signing key (flags 257) for example.net with key id 40692 and shows the matching DS record, which holds a 256-bit digest written in hexadecimal.
sections.plainLanguage: A DS record is like a short ID card for a key. This part says which fingerprint recipe to use to make the ID card.

sections.title: Sizes and Implementation Rules
sections.content:
The sizes are fixed. A GOST public key MUST be 512 bits, a GOST signature is 512 bits, and a GOST digest is 256 bits.

Support is optional: DNSSEC-aware implementations MAY support RRSIG and DNSKEY records made with the GOST algorithms. Any DNSSEC-GOST implementation, however, MUST support both NSEC and NSEC3 for proving that a name does not exist.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything has a set size, like a key that always fits one lock shape. Programs are allowed, but not forced, to know this recipe.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC estimates the resistance of GOST R 34.10-2001 at 2 to the power of 128 operations of multiple elliptic curve point computations on prime modulus of order 2 to the power of 256. For the GOST R 34.11-94 hash it also estimates 2 to the power of 128 operations. It notes a known method that reduces this to 2 to the power of 105 operations, but says the method needs the colliding message to be padded with 1024 random bit blocks of 256 bits each, so it cannot be used in any practical implementation.

For IANA, the document adds value 12 (mnemonic ECC-GOST, status OPTIONAL) to the DNS Security Algorithm Numbers registry, and adds digest type 3 (status OPTIONAL) for GOST R 34.11-94 to the DS digest types.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say breaking these locks would take an enormous amount of work. They also say that a known shortcut is too awkward to be used in real life.

items.label: ECC-GOST
items.desc: DNSSEC algorithm number for GOST R 34.10-2001; status OPTIONAL.
